title: Locking
lead: Lock compatibility, two-phase locking, strict locking and deadlock handling.
goals: Strict locking and the source schedule

sections.title: Lock modes and compatibility
sections.html:
A scheduler and its lock manager

A scheduler must decide as operations arrive; the full transaction may not be known. Pessimistic control protects objects before access, while optimistic control separates work and validates it later. Shared S locks permit reads; exclusive X locks protect writes. Different transactions can share S, but any X conflicts.

Held \ RequestedSX
SGrantWait
XWaitWait

A request is granted or queued, the transaction waits if denied, and release updates the lock table and may wake waiters. A lock upgrade S→X must wait for other holders too; already holding S does not grant an automatic right to write.

PDF pp. 1–4

Why locks alone are insufficient

The source lets T1 acquire X(A), read/write and release it; T2 then acquires X(A), writes and releases; T1 later reacquires S(A) and reads. Every individual access is locked, yet W1(A) precedes W2(A) and W2(A) precedes R1(A), creating a cycle. A protocol constraining when locks may be acquired and released is necessary in addition to mutual exclusion.

PDF pp. 5–6

sections.title: Two-phase locking
sections.html:
Two-phase locking

In the growing phase a transaction acquires locks and may upgrade them. Once it releases any lock, it enters the shrinking phase and cannot acquire new locks or upgrade. “Two phases” refers to this local lock lifecycle, not the two-phase commit protocol in lecture 22.

The earlier counterexample fails 2PL because T1 reacquires A after releasing it. In the valid source trace T1 retains X(A) across its second read, blocking T2 until release. 2PL ensures conflict serializability: ordering transactions by their last lock acquisition (lock point) respects the relevant conflict order. It is sufficient, not necessary; some serializable schedules cannot be generated by 2PL.

PDF pp. 7–10

Cascading aborts under basic 2PL

Basic 2PL can release a write lock before commit. T1 writes A, unlocks it and later aborts; T2 may have locked A, read that uncommitted value and written derived data. T2 must then abort too, even though both transactions followed the two phases. Dirty reads and cascading rollback concern recoverability; serializability alone does not remove them. Basic 2PL can also deadlock, which requires a separate policy.

PDF pp. 11–12

sections.title: Strict locking and the source schedule
sections.html:
Strict locking and simpler rollback

The source’s strict 2PL retains all locks until commit or abort (often called rigorous 2PL; a common narrower definition of strict 2PL retains all X locks). Readers cannot observe a writer’s uncommitted changes. An abort can restore original values before releasing locks without another transaction having depended on those values. The stronger rule avoids cascading aborts while retaining conflict serializability; it may block more work than an application needs.

PDF pp. 13–14

Transfer and total: 1900 versus 2000

Start A=B=1000. T1 transfers 100 from A to B, while T2 sums both. In the non-2PL trace T1 debits A and unlocks it before locking B; T2 reads A=900 and B=1000 before the credit, reporting 1900. T1’s later acquisition of B is the phase violation.

In basic 2PL, T1 acquires X(B) before releasing X(A). T2 may then read A but must wait for B until its credit is complete; it reports 2000. With the source’s strict rule, T1 keeps both locks to transaction completion and T2 reads the complete result afterward, again 2000. This compares the exact three source schedules rather than treating all lock use as equivalent.

PDF pp. 15–17

sections.title: Deadlock detection
sections.html:
Deadlock and the waits-for graph

Two transactions can each hold one needed lock and wait for the other. A waits-for edge Ti→Tj means Ti is currently blocked by a lock held by Tj; this is different from a serializability precedence edge. The three-transaction example has T1 holding S(A), T2 holding X(B), T3 holding S(C). Requests S1(B),X2(C),X3(A) give T1→T2→T3→T1.

Periodically detect cycles, select a victim and roll it back so its locks are released. Conservative/preclaiming 2PL instead obtains its entire required lock set before execution (or waits holding none), eliminating hold-and-wait, but requires advance knowledge and can reduce concurrency.

PDF pp. 18–21

Choosing a deadlock victim

Victim policy may consider age, progress, locks held, dependent transactions requiring cascading rollback and previous restarts to avoid starvation. Checking frequently costs CPU; checking rarely extends blocking. Aborting the youngest or least-progressed transaction is a policy choice, not a universal correctness rule.

PDF p. 22

sections.title: Wait-die and wound-wait
sections.html:
Wait–Die and Wound–Wait

Assign timestamps so older transactions have higher priority. On a conflicting request, compare the requester with the holder:

PolicyOlder requester, younger holderYounger requester, older holder
Wait–DieRequester waitsRequester aborts
Wound–WaitHolder abortsRequester waits

If older T1 requests A held by younger T2, Wait–Die lets T1 wait and Wound–Wait aborts T2. If younger T2 requests A held by older T1, Wait–Die aborts T2 and Wound–Wait makes it wait. Be precise about which transaction dies: Wait–Die aborts the requester; Wound–Wait can abort the holder.

PDF pp. 23–26

Why prevention works and why timestamps persist

Wait–Die permits waiting only from older to younger; Wound–Wait only from younger to older. A strictly ordered timestamp direction cannot form a cycle. A restarted transaction retains its original timestamp so it eventually becomes relatively old instead of repeatedly losing as a new youngest transaction. Locking plus a phase protocol provides serializability; detection or timestamp prevention handles liveness.

PDF pp. 27–28

quiz.question: T_old requests a lock held by T_new. What does wound-wait do?
options: T_new aborts and releases its locks
quiz.explanation: Under wound-wait, a transaction with a smaller timestamp can force a younger transaction holding the requested lock to abort.

source.summary: Lecture 20 covers shared and exclusive locks, 2PL, strict 2PL, deadlock detection, and the wait-die and wound-wait prevention rules.
